planting.note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; never use fertilized potting mix, garden soil, or tap water, all of which harm this plant.

directions: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; never use fertilized potting mix, garden soil, or tap water, all of which harm this plant. Long, narrow, strap-shaped leaves are covered in reddish, sticky, glandular tentacles that glisten with dewy droplets and slowly curl around any small insect unlucky enough to land and become trapped, one of the easiest and most forgiving carnivorous plants for beginners due to its tolerance of average humidity and simple care requirements compared to fussier carnivorous species. Native to nutrient-poor, seasonally wet fynbos habitat in South Africa's Cape region, it self-sows readily under good growing conditions, producing abundant fine seed and volunteer seedlings, and blooms with small pink flowers on tall stalks well above the sticky leaves. Keep the growing medium constantly moist with pure water, provide bright light for the best dew production, and feed occasionally with small insects if grown indoors away from a natural insect supply.
sources: North American Sarracenia and Carnivorous Plant Society reference

planting.note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; round-leaved sundew needs a cold winter dormancy with reduced light and moisture unlike tropical sundew species.

directions: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; round-leaved sundew needs a cold winter dormancy with reduced light and moisture unlike tropical sundew species. Small, round, red-tinged leaves form a low rosette covered in fine, glistening, sticky tentacles that trap and slowly digest tiny insects, the classic sundew of northern bogs found circumboreally across cold-temperate wetlands of North America, Europe, and Asia, historically the source species behind the plant's common name from its dewdrop-like glandular secretions. Unlike the tropical Cape sundew, it requires a genuine cold winter dormancy to survive long-term, going through a resting bud stage (hibernaculum) through the coldest months before resuming active growth in spring. Keep the growing medium constantly wet with pure water through the growing season, provide bright light, and allow the plant to go dormant naturally over winter without forcing continued growth.
sources: North American Sarracenia and Carnivorous Plant Society reference

planting.note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; spoonleaf sundew tolerates a wider range of climates than round-leaved sundew, from cold bogs to warm coastal plain seeps.

directions: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss kept in a tray of rain or distilled water; spoonleaf sundew tolerates a wider range of climates than round-leaved sundew, from cold bogs to warm coastal plain seeps. Narrow, spoon-shaped leaves tipped with sticky, glistening, red tentacles are often held semi-upright rather than lying flat, trapping small insects across the wet, sunny bogs, seeps, and pond margins where it grows natively across a wide range spanning from cold northern peatlands to warm Gulf coastal plain wetlands. Its broader climate tolerance compared to the more cold-dependent round-leaved sundew makes it a good choice for a bog garden across a wider range of USDA zones, including warmer Southern climates where round-leaved sundew struggles without a hard winter. Keep the growing medium constantly wet with pure water, provide bright light for the best coloring and dew production, and allow a period of reduced growth over winter even in milder climates.
sources: North American Sarracenia and Carnivorous Plant Society reference

planting.note: Set transplants into a well-drained, mineral-rich carnivorous plant mix (equal parts perlite, sand, and peat) kept evenly moist with rain or distilled water; Mexican butterworts tolerate slightly richer, better-drained conditions than bog-dwelling sundews and pitcher plants.

directions: Set transplants into a well-drained, mineral-rich carnivorous plant mix (equal parts perlite, sand, and peat) kept evenly moist with rain or distilled water; Mexican butterworts tolerate slightly richer, better-drained conditions than bog-dwelling sundews and pitcher plants. Broad, flat, pale yellow-green leaves coated in a glistening, sticky film trap and slowly digest small insects that land on the leaf surface, one of the largest-leaved of the Mexican butterwort species, producing showy, tall-stemmed purple flowers in season that add ornamental value beyond the plant's carnivorous foliage. Native to limestone cliffs and seasonally moist rock outcrops in Mexico, it tolerates a brief dry season better than bog-dwelling carnivorous plants, going through a smaller, more compact winter rosette (a succulent, non-carnivorous form) during its natural dry dormant period. Reduce watering somewhat in winter to allow the natural dormant rosette to form, resume regular moist conditions in spring as new growth emerges, and provide bright, indirect light rather than harsh direct sun.
sources: North American Sarracenia and Carnivorous Plant Society reference
